Freedom has a price

lines.text: Half of covered workers are in a pricier PPO. Why?
lines.say: Half of covered workers are in a pricier PPO. Why?

lines.text: In 2026, only 12% were in an HMO, per KFF. So what's the difference?
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, only twelve percent were in an HMO, per KFF. So what's the difference?

lines.text: An HMO usually covers only its network, except emergencies, and often needs a referral for a specialist.
lines.say: An HMO usually covers only its network, except emergencies, and often needs a referral for a specialist.

lines.text: A PPO lets you go outside the network without a referral, but you pay more.
lines.say: A PPO lets you go outside the network without a referral, but you pay more.

lines.text: In 2026, PPO single premiums averaged $10,272 versus $9,804 for all plans, per KFF.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, PPO single premiums averaged about ten thousand three hundred dollars, versus about ninety-eight hundred for all plans, per KFF.

lines.text: Our math: family PPO coverage cost $1,219 more a year than average, employer and worker shares combined.

lines.text: Meanwhile, HMOs fell from 19% of covered workers in 2019 to 12% in 2025.
lines.say: Meanwhile, HMOs fell from nineteen percent of covered workers in twenty nineteen to twelve percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That's the trade-off: an HMO limits choices, while a PPO sells freedom at a higher price.

post.title: HMO vs PPO: why half of covered workers pay more for a PPO
post.ig:
In 2026, 50% of workers with job coverage were in a PPO. Only 12% were in an HMO (KFF changed its plan categories in 2026).
An HMO usually covers only its network (except emergencies) and often needs referrals; a PPO covers out-of-network care at a higher cost.
KFF 2026: PPO single premiums averaged $10,272 vs $9,804 for all plans. Our math: family PPO coverage ran $1,219 more than average.
HMO share fell from 19% in 2019 to 12% in 2025.
Sources: KFF Employer Health Benefits Surveys 2016-2026; HealthCare.gov.
